title: What is stagflation?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain stagflation, a combination of high unemployment, slow economic growth, and high inflation. They cover the history behind it: the Phillips curve and its supposed inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation, the 1960s Fed policy of keeping unemployment artificially low, the wage-price spiral, the 1973 oil embargo, and the 1970s stagflation under Carter with inflation peaking near 13.3 percent in 1979. They describe Paul Volcker's shift at the Fed to monetary tightening based on Milton Friedman's ideas, the recession that followed, and how Friedman-style policies were tested in Chile. They compare 2011 inflation worries to the 1970s and discuss deflation and who benefits from fixed debt. The episode ends with a listener mail from Jason in Baltimore about a childhood Green Machine accident.

segments.title: Opening banter and intro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on econ and joke about money and Chuck's interest in economics. Josh mentions a article warning of rampant inflation in 2011.

segments.title: Inflation basics and recent inflation figures
segments.summary: They explain supply and demand as applied to money and inflation, cite food and airline price rises, and note that the USDA projected about one percent food cost inflation. They discuss why mild inflation is considered healthy and why hyperinflation is bad.

segments.title: Defining stagflation
segments.summary: Josh says stagflation is the worst outcome: high unemployment and slow growth combined with high inflation. Chuck gives inflation statistics, including the July 2008 peak of 5.6 percent and negative 0.3 percent average in 2009. They also note that deflation makes savings more valuable.

segments.title: Vicious cycle and the 1970s malaise
segments.summary: They explain how stagflation forms a vicious cycle of shrinking dollars, unemployment, and sluggish growth. They mention Carter's malaise and the idea that recessions correct an economy, using a forest and underbrush analogy. The term is a contraction of stagnant and inflation.

segments.title: Phillips curve and the 1960s Fed
segments.summary: Keynesian economics predicted inflation rises with demand, and the Phillips curve links low unemployment to higher inflation. The Fed in the 1960s tried to keep unemployment artificially low, accepting higher inflation, which led to a wage-price spiral.

segments.title: Oil embargo and 1970s inflation peak
segments.summary: The wage-price spiral, combined with the 1973 oil embargo, drove inflation up. Inflation hit 5.5 percent in 1970, 12.2 percent in 1974, and peaked at 13.3 percent around 1979. Carter faced hostages in Iran, lines at gas pumps, and a stock market that lost value after inflation.

segments.title: Volcker, Friedman, and monetary tightening
segments.summary: Paul Volcker, as Fed head in 1979, shifted policy toward Friedman's monetarist ideas, reducing money supply and raising interest rates. The recession that followed was painful but stabilized inflation. Friedman's ideas were tested in Chile under Pinochet.

segments.title: Current Fed policy and debt
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of timing interest rate changes, the risk that waiting too long causes inflation, and the irony that Friedman's policies confirmed the Phillips curve. They close the topic by noting that fixed debt is best to owe when inflation is high.

segments.title: Closing and promotions
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh close the episode and point listeners to the stagflation article on HowStuffWorks.
